title: Creating, Opening, and Removing Files through the Command Line
summary: Covers mkdir, touch, open, pwd, rm, rm with a wildcard, and rm -r, with a strong warning about how destructive removal commands are.

concepts.heading: Creating
points: mkdir name creates a directory in the current location; cd into it and ls shows it is empty.
touch name.ext creates an empty file (e.g. touch Text2.txt), far quicker than making one in an editor and saving it.
(Extra) touch on an existing file only updates its timestamp.

concepts.heading: Opening files (macOS)
points: open file opens it with the default application.
open -a AppName file opens it in a chosen application via the -a flag.
(Extra) Git Bash on Windows uses start file instead; the cheat sheet in the reference repo lists start.

concepts.heading: Knowing where you are
points: The prompt shows the current folder name; pwd (print working directory) prints the full path.
Check location before any destructive command.

concepts.heading: Removing
points: rm file deletes a file, and the deletion bypasses any trash bin.
rm * uses the * wildcard to match every file in the current directory, so it only works as intended in the right folder.
rm folder alone fails with a message that the target is a directory.
rm -r folder removes a directory and everything inside it (the -r flag means recursive).
Windows/Git Bash and Mac behave the same for these commands.

concepts.heading: Danger
points: The GUI offers safeguards that the command line lacks.

sudo runs a command with admin rights; -f forces removal with no confirmation; combining sudo rm -rf with a root target wipes a disk irrecoverably. Never run it. The online story shown in the lecture was a hoax, but the command is real.
Further reading: the free 'Learn Enough Command Line to Be Dangerous' tutorial (covers grep, curl and more).

code_examples.caption: Full workflow
code_examples.code:
mkdir Angela
cd Angela
touch Text2.txt
open Text2.txt
open -a TextEdit Text2.txt
pwd
rm Text2.txt
touch a.txt b.txt c.txt
rm *
cd ..
rm -r Angela

task.name: Make and delete files via the terminal
task.starting_point: Terminal in a scratch location (never your home or root for deletes).
task.goal: Create a folder, put files in it, open one, then clean everything up.
steps: mkdir a new folder and cd into it.
touch several .txt files and ls to confirm.
open one in the default app, then in a chosen app with -a.
Remove one file with rm, then all with rm *.
cd .. and delete the folder with rm -r.
task.expected_result: Folder and files appear in Finder/Explorer as created, and disappear when removed.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 21 - The Unix Command Line/The Unix Command Line.txt

pitfalls: rm * in the wrong directory deletes the wrong files.
Never combine sudo, -rf and a root path.

gaps_and_ideas: Proposed new lesson 'Creating and removing files'. Blurb: mkdir and touch create folders and empty files, open (macOS) or start (Git Bash) opens them, pwd confirms where you are, and rm / rm -r delete permanently with no trash bin.

Tasks: (1) mkdir a project folder and cd into it; (2) touch index.html styles.css script.js in one command and ls to confirm; (3) run pwd and copy the printed path into an answer box; (4) remove one file with rm; (5) cd .. and remove the folder, first trying plain rm to see the 'is a directory' error, then rm -r.
Starter code idea: extend the fake file-tree object from the navigation lesson with commands mkdir, touch, pwd, rm, rm *, rm -r, so learners keep the same tree across lessons.

Interactive demo / safety layer: the simulator refuses rm on a folder without -r (showing the real error text pattern), asks for confirmation when rm * is run in ~, and shows an explanatory warning card (never executing) if someone types sudo rm -rf /.
